newsitem.title: FRANCE: Lacroix's magic woos Paris fashion crowd.
newsitem.headline: Lacroix's magic woos Paris fashion crowd.

text.p: French couturier Christian Lacroix dreamed up wildly luxurious mixes of textiles and textures with a Far Eastern flavour for the 10th anniversary of his fashion house on Tuesday, winning the loudest applause of the season.

Organza, satin, taffeta, tulle and lace -- each dress was a sumptuous collage of fabrics and genres as Lacroix embarked on a lone, mad voyage into a universe of imaginary women. The clothes were in fact more the work of an immensely imaginative artist than a dressmaker -- beautiful to look at but hard to wear.
Like a magician, he crafted saffron, pomegranate, flame and tearose silks into ornately draped gowns, many embroidered with gold and jewels worthy of a maharanee.

Dutch model Karen Mulder, in one of her rare appearances of this spring-summer season, swept out in a magnificent strapless irridescent apricot gown astonishingly draped into three tiers, while Carla Bruni, floated down the catwalk in pale and misty aqua, puffed and smocked beneath a delicate corseted bustier.

Lacroix's genius also lay in the detail: gold embroidered bellbottoms peeking out from beneath a gown strewn with red and pink roses or the tiny flowers slanting down a gold lace bodice, joining it to a skirt that glowed peach then mauve in the light.

"Women are always looking for individuality and freedom," Lacroix told a crowd of admirers after the show. "It's not because there's a dictatorship that says everything should be black or Zen that it should be obeyed. Women want to be themselves and our duty is to give them that."
Italian actress Claudia Cardinale said: "I think he has great vitality, designs, colours. He is Mediterranean like I am, very open, nice and smiling. But I usually wear Armani."
The Duchess of York, mobbed by paparazzi, ruled out any buying. "No, no, no," she said. "I think he's a great designer but I'm just just here to take in knowledge.
Germany's Karl Lagerfeld went to the other extreme for Chanel with styling for the emaciated embodying pure refinement.

Lagerfeld, who has succeeded during his 14 years at Chanel in staying faithful to the label's spirit while bringing it modern touches, unveiled skinny glove-fitting black jackets, free of ornament but for pearl buttons or a diamond clasp.
Over wide trousers of featherweight fluid wool or narrow, translucent skirts of black chiffon with wave-edged hemlines at mid-calf, they formed dark, sinewy silhouettes.
It was pure class with an edgy restraint, from the white cuffs of a pert organza blouse beneath a trademark tweed and the wide-brimmed straw hats curtained with black widow mesh.
But the show begged the question of what happens to those nervous, slim silhouettes when the fashions are donned by Chanel's matronly customers.

Evening came with a 1920s flavour in tube beading on smoky, diaphanous chiffon, a series of slim terracotta tulle gowns with jet embroidery and the feathers perched on slim wire ornaments wobbling on the supermodels' hair.
"It was absolutely amazing. The height of refinement. The scalloping, the edging, the make-up -- everything was perfect," said Joseph Boitano of U.S. department stores Bergdorf Goodman.
"That's how a couture customer wants to look," he added.
Kiki Feraud fastened gold bibs on African motif crepes, rows of brass buttons on a bellbottomed jumpsuit and table napkins on a creamy skirt for her father's couture label.
Like the military jackets with gold braid, Fortuny-pleated silver gown with bumpy seams and over-sized Aladdin turbans of crumpled gauze, the collection cried out for a lighter touch.
